newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS-Unidanmark profits down, costs up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Unidanmark profits down, costs up.

text.p: Danish bank group Unidanmark on Wednesday announced a fall in 1996 profits and a rise in costs, but said it was making strategic investments to carve out a strong position in a more integrated Nordic market.
Reporting a slightly greater-than-expected slip in operating profits to 2.801 billion crowns ($433.8 million) from 2.969 billion crowns in 1995, the bank saw little short-term improvement.
"Unibank anticipates continuing strong competition in 1997. Net interest and fees receivable are expected to remain largely unchanged," the report said.
Analysts had, on average, forecast an operating profit of 2.912 billion crowns.
Unidanmark said expenses grew in 1996 by 183 million crowns to 5.8 billion and were likely to be similar in 1997.

It added that expenses, depreciation and amortisation together accounted for 72 percent of profit before expenses, excluding investment portfolio income, but it aimed to reduce its cost-income ratio "on an ongoing basis."
The bank said the rise in costs was money well spent on securing the group's position in what it expected to be a progressively regional financial market.

The bulk of the rise, 144 million crowns, went on the acquisition of Swedish-Swiss Asea Brown Boveri's stockbroking business and the subsequent establishment of Aros Securities as a Nordic investment banking unit of Unidanmark.
More costs were incurred by the opening of a branch office in Stockholm, the bank said, adding that it planned to open Oslo and Helsinki branch offices in the summer of 1997.
"Unibank's strategy is to attain a prominent position in the Nordic financial services markets, which are projected to become increasingly integrated in the years to come."
"The setting up of branches will strengthen Unibank's provision of credit and payments transmission services to its Nordic corporate customers," the bank said.

The local stock market, however, focused on the weaker bottom line and a dividend frozen at 10 percent because of what the Unidanmark report called a "not quite satisfactory" return on equity of 13 percent.
"Unidanmark's result was a bit lower than expectations, but what strikes us is that the dividend has not been raised," a dealer who declined to be named told Reuters.
"This is definitely going to disappoint foreign investors," he added.
But after swinging between a high of 363 crowns and a low of 348, the bank's shares ended the day at 355 crowns, unchanged from Wednesday's close and Thursday's opening level.
The report made no prediction for 1997's bottom line but said it expected its bank and mortgage lending to continue growing, although at a slower rate than in 1996.
It said it expected loan loss provisions to be somewhat lower, contingent on continued favourable macroeconomic development. ($ = 6.457 Danish Crowns)
